title: Capitol Hill Erupts Over Trump-Backed Reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
snippet: Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are launching aggressive inquiries into Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang following White House intervention, citing grave national security risks and potential chip export violations to China.
content:
WASHINGTON — Lawmakers on Capitol Hill unleashed a wave of bipartisan criticism Monday following Nvidia’s sudden decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, a move heavily encouraged by President Donald Trump that has ignited fresh concerns over national security and potential ethical lapses at the epicenter of America’s artificial intelligence boom.

The semiconductor giant's board brought Huang back into the fold after Trump publicly voiced support for his return. However, the decision has only amplified congressional scrutiny surrounding Huang’s acknowledged ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative and ongoing allegations that Nvidia violated U.S. export controls by routing cutting-edge AI chips to Beijing.

Subpoenas and Hearings on the Horizon

Outgoing Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced Monday that Huang has been called to testify publicly before the panel on Dec. 3. Meanwhile, incoming committee chair Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., called on the administration to explain its intervention, characterizing the White House's pressure tactics as deeply reckless.

In the House, incoming Oversight Committee Chairman Robert Garcia, D-Calif., signaled that lawmakers would aggressively investigate the circumstances surrounding Trump's direct involvement in corporate decision-making at Nvidia.

"This raises serious national security and corruption questions," Garcia stated, emphasizing that Congress intends to examine the White House's actions thoroughly.

National Security Risks and Export Control Questions

Nvidia, currently a dominant force in the global AI market, was already under intense congressional investigation after Huang confirmed a personal relationship with Alice Huang, CEO of Megaspeed, who U.S. intelligence officials suspect of acting as a spy for Beijing.

Bipartisan leadership across several House panels—including Select Committee on China Chair John Moolenaar, R-Mich., House Intelligence Chair Rick Crawford, R-Ark., and House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla.—issued a stern joint statement maintaining that Nvidia's internal review does not resolve the looming national security implications.

"We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities," the chairmen stated.

Concerns also extend to the executive branch, where Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently expressed frustration over delays within the Commerce Department, led by Secretary Howard Lutnick, regarding export restrictions aimed at curbing chip sales to foreign entities linked to Chinese intelligence.

Bipartisan Backlash Across Both Parties

While executive branch officials sought to downplay national security risks, lawmakers from both political parties voiced skepticism over how the board determined Huang posed no security threat.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, publicly questioned whether federal law enforcement had conducted proper defensive briefings before clearing Huang, while retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., warned that supplying advanced microprocessors to China undermines Washington's strategic goals in the global AI race.

Democrats, who are set to assume committee leadership roles in January, pledged to broaden their oversight into both executive corruption and national security breaches. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., upcoming chair of the Senate Finance Committee, declared that under the current administration, "our national security is for sale," promising robust accountability measures when the new Congress convenes next year.
